summary.title: The Six Dumbest Ideas in Computer Security
summary.one_liner: Marcus Ranum's essay argues that common security practices like default-permit, enumerating badness, and penetrate-and-patch are fundamentally flawed, and that default-deny, enumerating goodness, and secure-by-design engineering work better.
keywords: why do security bugs keep appearing
takeaways: Default-permit policies (allow everything unless known bad) lead to endless arms races; default-deny is the better baseline.
Enumerating badness (blacklists such as antivirus signatures) cannot keep up with the volume of new malware; enumerating the small set of known-good software is more tractable.
Penetrate-and-patch treats security as trial-and-error fixes; systems should be designed to be secure and flaw-tolerant from the start.
Educating users and relying on early adopters are weak substitutes for removing the risky default behaviour in the first place.
summary.summary: This is a long opinion essay by Marcus Ranum listing six 'anti-good' ideas in computer security, ordered from most to least frequently seen. Each idea gets a section with examples from his experience, such as firewall rules, a load-balancer configured to deny by default, log analysis using 'artificial ignorance', and email attachment quarantine. The essay mostly argues from reasoning and anecdote rather than measured data, and it includes a few rough figures such as antivirus signature counts and industry estimates of new malware per month. It closes with a brief list of lesser dumb ideas, such as 'We're Not a Target'.
